steps.path: Contribute to YouCoded, and the bug and feature ticket screens
steps.headline: The contract, graded — accept these verdicts?

rows.statement: The walkthrough of how contributing works lives inside Contribute to YouCoded, not on the Development list.
rows.evidence: Checked on screen: the Development list has no walkthrough on it, and 'How contributing works' opens inside Contribute. Both halves are now pinned by tests.

rows.statement: The walkthrough explains contributing in plain words: describe it, review the design, try it, run checks, then choose to propose it.
rows.evidence: All five steps are there, in order, each with its own explanation, numbered and indented. Re-photographed after a fix that had been clipping the numbers.

rows.statement: Nothing becomes a public proposal until you approve it at the last step of the walkthrough.
rows.evidence: Step 5 says only your explicit approval sends a public proposal, and nothing in the code publishes anything without it.

rows.statement: The walkthrough has no gray warning box under its five steps.
rows.note: just delete the wierd warning in the gray box. what is "workspace details"? "set up separate workspace"? why not jsut "set up development workspace"?
rows.evidence: The gray warning box under the steps is gone — nothing sits between step 5 and the button.

rows.statement: Contribute to YouCoded leads with one sentence about its purpose and one setup action.
rows.evidence: The screen opens with its purpose and one setup button. Note: the purpose is three sentences, not one — but it is the paragraph in the picture you approved.

rows.statement: The setup action is a full-width main button like the app's other dialogs, with no caption beneath it.
rows.evidence: Full-width button in the app's normal style, with nothing written underneath it.

rows.statement: The same full-width button sits under the five walkthrough steps.
rows.evidence: The same button sits under the five steps when they are open.

rows.statement: The Contribute screen matches the app's other settings pages: short text, clear headings, evenly sized buttons.
rows.note: this is also just ugly, too much text, poor visual heirarchy, weirdly sized buttons. doesn't match our other settings pages.
rows.evidence: Yours to judge — this is the 'too much text, weirdly sized buttons' note you wrote, and whether it is fixed is your eye, not a test.

rows.statement: Setup leaves an existing development folder untouched and explains that the new project is separate.
rows.threshold: an existing folder is unchanged after setup runs in a dev instance
rows.evidence: Setup walks past any folder that already exists and creates a new one. Proven by putting a file in the way: it came back untouched, byte for byte.

rows.statement: You can start working in the new project on this device even when its backup has not connected.
rows.threshold: setup finishes and the project opens with backup unavailable
rows.evidence: You can finish setup and open the project with no backup connected. See the second question at the end — half of what you picked here no longer applies.

rows.statement: A ticket starts with the error and app version; recent logs are only included when you choose them.
rows.evidence: The ticket opens with the error that sent you there and your real app version; logs are only read when you tick the box.

rows.statement: You can write, review and send a ticket without any AI help; asking an assistant is a separate choice.
rows.evidence: A ticket can be written, reviewed and sent with no AI involved. Pinned by a test that fails if sending ever calls a provider.

rows.statement: You prepare and review a ticket in YouCoded, then finish attaching approved screenshots or files in GitHub.
rows.evidence: Choosing to attach files finishes the ticket in your browser, where you attach them — and it no longer files the ticket first, which used to break this for anyone signed in.

rows.statement: Before you attach a file, the screen says GitHub uploads it immediately, before you submit the ticket.
rows.evidence: Before you attach anything, the screen says GitHub uploads a file the moment it is attached.

rows.statement: The ticket screen opens with an editable title and description, a public-sharing notice, and optional error details.
rows.evidence: The ticket opens with an editable title and description, the public-on-GitHub notice, and optional error details.

rows.statement: Both the bug tab and the feature tab sit under one heading: Submit a ticket.
rows.evidence: Both tabs sit under one heading, 'Submit a ticket'.

rows.statement: Optional AI help appears only on the review step, behind a disclosure you open yourself.
rows.evidence: Every AI action is behind the 'Optional AI help' disclosure you open yourself — nothing AI-related is in the footer.

rows.statement: The ticket's optional evidence sits in three plain rows under one heading, each explained by the (i) on its row.
rows.evidence: Three plain rows under one heading, each explained by its own (i), with no gray sub-labels. This one broke once and is now pinned by the rule, not the wording.

rows.statement: The ticket screens use the same compact rows as other settings menus, without dense blocks of text.
rows.note: there's way too much poorly organized copy with unclear visual heirarchy. we need to simplify this and make it better match existing settings menus.
rows.evidence: Yours to judge — your 'poorly organized copy, unclear hierarchy' note, and whether it now matches the app's other settings menus.

rows.statement: Review ticket is a full-width main button that stays inactive until you have typed a title and description.
rows.evidence: Review ticket stays inactive until you have typed both a title and a description, and the screen now says what is missing.

rows.statement: No preview or mockup captions appear anywhere; Submit is the main button with Back to draft beneath it.
rows.evidence: No preview or mockup captions anywhere, and the footer is exactly two stacked buttons: Submit, then Back to draft.

rows.statement: Error details shows your real app version rather than a line saying nothing was collected.
rows.evidence: The version line is your real app version, read from the app itself. It used to be a made-up string.

rows.statement: If sending a ticket fails, your title, description and chosen details stay in the draft and you can retry.
rows.evidence: A failed send keeps your title, description and chosen details, and offers a retry. Proven by making the send fail and reading the fields back.

steps.path: Settings → Development → Report a Bug · Optional AI help
steps.headline: Should your assistant be able to try fixing the bug itself?
steps.today: The screen you are replacing had a second button: Let Claude Try to Fix It. It set up the workspace, opened a session, and handed the bug over. Your approved design has no such button — it was never on any deck, because I only found it while deleting the old screen.
steps.problem: Deleting a working feature nobody asked me to remove would be the kind of change you cannot trace back to anything. So I carried it over rather than drop it quietly — but that means there is UI in front of you that you never approved, which is the other thing I am not supposed to do.
steps.proposal: It now sits inside Optional AI help, under Improve wording, with a line saying it uses a lot of your model allowance. It files nothing and sends nothing. Three ways to go.

options.label: Keep it where it is
pros: Nothing is lost that the old screen could do.
It is behind the disclosure, so it does not crowd the two main buttons.
It reuses a workspace you already set up instead of downloading a second copy.
cons: It is a second AI action on a screen whose approved picture had one.
It spends a lot of your model allowance, and someone may press it without reading the line.

options.label: Cut it
pros: The screen is exactly the one you signed, with nothing added.
One fewer expensive action to explain.
cons: A working feature disappears from your app with no replacement.
The path from 'I found a bug' to 'try fixing it' goes away entirely.

options.label: Keep it, but show me a design first
pros: You decide how it looks and what it says before it ships.
cons: Another review round before this can merge.

steps.headline: Half of an answer you gave has quietly stopped applying — is that alright?
steps.today: You chose that setup should let you start on this device even when backup has not connected. That option also promised a visible warning saying so, and a way to retry connecting it.
steps.problem: Since then we found that putting the workspace where the app syncs things would push about a gigabyte of source code to your backup. So it now goes somewhere outside the synced area. That removes the risk — but it also means backup can never fail here, so there is nothing to warn about and nothing to retry. Half of what you picked no longer exists, and I would rather tell you than let you find it.
steps.proposal: Nothing on this screen mentions backup at all, which is what you asked for separately when you said not to mess with the sync system.

options.label: Leave it — nothing to warn about
pros: The screen stays as short as you approved it.
Nothing is uploaded, so no promise about backup can be broken.
Your other projects behave the same way; this one is not special.
cons: The workspace is not backed up, and the screen never says so.
If you later expect to find it on another computer, it will not be there.

options.label: Say once that it lives on this device
pros: You are told where the project lives at the moment it is created.
cons: Adds a line about backup to a screen you asked to keep clear of it.
It would be the only project in the app that explains its own backup status.
